summary: Defines three new DHCP options that deliver configuration information to clients of Novell Directory Services, such as which servers and directory tree to use. This lets such clients configure themselves automatically when joining a network.

eli5.summary: When a computer joins a network, it gets handed a note with what it needs. This adds the right note for one particular company's directory system.

questions: dhcp options for novell directory services
how does dhcp configure nds clients
what is the nds context option
subtitle: Three DHCP options that tell a Novell Directory Services client which servers, tree and context to use.

tldr.problem: An NDS client must find an NDS server and a starting point in the directory, which used to need manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: Three DHCP options carry a list of NDS servers (code 85), the NDS tree name (code 86) and the initial NDS context (code 87).
tldr.outcome: Together the options give a client enough information to connect to an NDS tree without manual configuration. DHCP itself offers no authentication, so a rogue DHCP server could misdirect clients.

today: RFC 2241 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why NDS Needs DHCP Options
sections.content:
Novell Directory Services (NDS) is a distributed, replicated, hierarchical database of objects such as nodes, services, users and applications. An NDS client must find an NDS server to authenticate and reach the database, and it helps if the client starts in the part of the database the user cares about.

This RFC defines DHCP options to carry that information to TCP/IP clients of NDS: the NDS Servers Option, the NDS Tree Name Option and the NDS Context Option.

The tree name and context are 16-bit Unicode text sent as UTF-8. Plain 7-bit ASCII is unchanged by UTF-8, so ASCII-only clients and servers can support the options when names are restricted to ASCII.
sections.eli5: A new computer on the network does not know where the company phone book is kept. DHCP hands it three notes: who to call, which phone book, and which page to open.

sections.title: The Server List and Tree Name Options
sections.content:
The NDS Servers Option has code 85. It lists one or more NDS servers, each as a four-octet address, in order of preference (SHOULD). The minimum length is 4 octets and the length MUST be a multiple of 4.

The NDS Tree Name Option has code 86 and names the tree the client will contact. The name is UTF-8 encoded and should not be zero terminated. The maximum length is 255 bytes.
sections.eli5: Option 85 is a list of phone numbers in order of who to try first. Option 86 is the name of the phone book.

sections.title: The Context Option and Long Names
sections.content:
The NDS Context Option has code 87 and gives the initial context the client should use, again as UTF-8 text that should not be zero terminated.

A single DHCP option holds at most 255 octets, but a context name can be longer. So the option may appear more than once in the packet, and the contents of all instances are concatenated, as suggested in the DHCP specification, to form the full context. A single encoded character could be split between two instances. Implementations are discouraged from enforcing any specific maximum on the final concatenated context.
sections.eli5: If the page number is too long to fit on one note, it is written on several notes and you join them together in order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: DHCP provides no authentication or security mechanisms of its own. These options allow an unauthorized DHCP server to misdirect an NDS client to a nonexistent NDS server or even a spoof one. The RFC says these threats are similar to what NDS faces in its native IPX environment.
sections.eli5: If a stranger hands out the notes, they can send you to the wrong place, because the notes are not signed.

items.label: NDS Servers
items.desc: List of four-octet server addresses; length a multiple of 4, minimum 4.

items.label: NDS Context
items.desc: UTF-8 initial context; may repeat, with up to 255 octets each.
